summary: Phenylalanine is an essential aromatic amino acid that the body cannot synthesize and must obtain from dietary protein. It is a building block of proteins and the precursor of tyrosine, catecholamines, thyroid hormone and melanin. It is a normal component of parenteral and enteral amino-acid (nutrition) formulations and is also one of the two amino acids in the artificial sweetener aspartame. It is not a conventional FDA-approved drug; it is treated here as a nutritional component. The critical safety issue is phenylketonuria (PKU), an inherited inability to metabolize phenylalanine: in PKU, dietary phenylalanine must be strictly restricted to prevent neurotoxic accumulation. For this reason, aspartame-containing products in the US carry the labeling statement 'Phenylketonurics: Contains Phenylalanine.'

moa: Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid incorporated into proteins during translation. It is hydroxylated by phenylalanine hydroxylase (with tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor) to tyrosine, which is the precursor of dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroid hormones and melanin. In phenylketonuria, deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity causes phenylalanine and its phenylketone metabolites to accumulate, which is neurotoxic if intake is not restricted.

preg: Phenylalanine is a required nutrient in pregnancy as part of normal protein intake. The key concern is maternal PKU: elevated maternal blood phenylalanine is teratogenic and can cause microcephaly, congenital heart disease, growth restriction and intellectual disability in the infant, so phenylalanine must be tightly controlled before and throughout pregnancy. Aspartame in normal dietary amounts is considered acceptable in pregnancy for women without PKU.
lact: Phenylalanine is a normal constituent of breast milk and is required nutritionally. Women with PKU should continue dietary phenylalanine control while breastfeeding under metabolic supervision. Aspartame in usual amounts is considered acceptable during breastfeeding for women without PKU.
renal: Amino-acid (and therefore phenylalanine) intake in parenteral/enteral nutrition is adjusted according to renal function and overall protein needs in nutrition support; no specific concern for dietary phenylalanine in normal renal function.
hepatic: In advanced liver disease and hepatic encephalopathy, aromatic amino acids including phenylalanine may be restricted (and branched-chain amino acids favored) as part of specialized nutrition; otherwise no specific restriction.

major: None as a normal nutrient; in PKU, any high-phenylalanine source (high-protein foods, aspartame) is detrimental
moderate: Large neutral amino acids compete for the same transporter and can modestly affect phenylalanine uptake (used therapeutically in some PKU regimens)

missed: Not applicable in the usual sense - phenylalanine is supplied through diet or nutrition formulas rather than as scheduled doses. In managed PKU diets, follow the metabolic team's plan; do not attempt to 'make up' intake, and keep to prescribed protein-substitute schedules.
overdose: Excessive phenylalanine is clinically important mainly in phenylketonuria, where high intake leads to neurotoxic accumulation; management is dietary restriction with metabolic supervision and monitoring of blood phenylalanine. In normal individuals, ordinary dietary or aspartame intake does not cause toxicity. Inappropriate parenteral amino-acid administration is managed by adjusting the nutrition regimen and supportive care.
